transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Rivera (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (HeliosPay CTO), Samir Patel (HeliosPay Infra), Renee Cho (HeliosPay ML), Tom Alvarez (HeliosPay SRE)

Summary: High-level technical deep dive focused on autoscaling behavior for HeliosPay's mixed-latency payment flows. Discussed priority queueing for high-value requests, warmup strategies for reserved GPU pools, KV cache impacts on tail latency, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps to run a burst simulation using HeliosPay's real traffic profile and to scope Reserved GPU POC.

Topics: autoscale policy design, prewarmed pool sizing, queue priorities, backpressure, KV cache TTL and prefix caching, quantization (8-bit/4-bit) latency vs accuracy tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment constraints, observability hooks for p95/p99/latency budgets.

=== Transcript ===
[00:00] Maya Chen: all right everybody thanks for joining on a Saturday i appreciate it, um we'll run through, this is a technical deep dive so feel free to interrupt. Diego and Olivia from my side will cover the runtime and the warmup strategy details. Aisha, Samir, Renee, Tom, do you want to intro briefly?
[00:05] Aisha Khan: yeah sure, hi everyone, i'm aisha, CTO at HeliosPay. We're evaluating Redwood for authorizations and customer support smart replies, also some higher-value reconciliation flows. Our main worry is spikes at end-of-day and large-batch reconciliation that creates backpressure. We need p95 latency under 150ms for authorizations.
[00:20] Samir Patel: samir here, infra. We run a mixed fleet, some on GCP, some on-prem colo for compliance. We expect bursts from webhook spikes, and we need a model for reserved capacity plus burst.
[00:25] Renee Cho: renee - ml, i'm focused on quality: we can't degrade the model outputs by aggressive quantization on authorization rulings. But low-latency phases (support chat) can be quantized more.
[00:32] Tom Alvarez: tom - SRE. Observability and tracing are critical; we'll need token-level latency to tie to alerts.
[00:35] Diego Rivera: great, thanks all. quick agenda: 1) autoscale and priority queues, 2) prewarm strategies for reserved GPU pools and ephemeral burst, 3) kv cache impacts and warmup, 4) quantization and warm-start tradeoffs, 5) ops and observability hooks.

[02:10] Diego Rivera: first, priority queueing - HeliosPay has mixed SLAs, correct? authorizations are high-priority, support chat is lower. Our recommendation: run two logical queues per pool - priority and best-effort - with tokenized admission control. Priority requests get prewarmed slots and bypass long queue lengths up to a small concurrency cap. Best-effort flows use a separate queue with batching optimizations to maximize throughput.
[02:42] Renee Cho: how do you ensure that priority bypass doesn't starve the best-effort queue under sustained medium load?
[02:45] Diego Rivera: good question. We implement a leaky-bucket style token reservoir for priority tokens. Tokens refill at a rate tied to the reserved pool capacity and SLO headroom. Once the token budget is depleted, high-priority gets degraded to the same admission as best-effort or can be routed to a lower-cost quantized model variant. This gives deterministic headroom.
[03:12] Samir Patel: what about burst queues - should we rely on ephemeral prewarmed pods or a burst queue that blocks? Our security team prefers reserved capacity because of data residency.
[03:18] Olivia Park: you can combine both: reserved prewarmed pool for the critical subset (authorizations) sized for normal peak + small headroom, plus ephemeral burst instances in a trusted VPC when you need extra. For HeliosPay we can scope a hybrid where ephemeral burst is restricted to certain regions/VMs and audited via your KMS.

[04:05] Aisha Khan: can you walk through the warmup timeline? we saw weird p99 spikes on first cold request in past tests.
[04:09] Diego Rivera: yes. The runtime has three warm states: cold (startup, large JIT/weight load), warm (weights in GPU memory, caches cold), and prewarmed (kv cache, prefix cache, compiled kernels hot). Cold to warm is dominated by model load and memory allocation — tens of seconds for big models on GPU unless you pre-stage images. Warm to prewarmed depends on KV cache hits and sequence history; we use traffic-driven warmup via replay of synthetic prefixes or by opportunistic caching from recent requests. Typical times: cold->warm 20-45s, warm->prewarmed 1-5s of sustained prefix hits for short contexts, but depends on token length and kv cache TTL.
[04:45] Tom Alvarez: so prewarmed pools are basically GPUs with warmed KV caches; how do you size the prewarm TTL so caches remain useful but not stale?
[04:51] Diego Rivera: TTLs are workload-driven. For short-lived user sessions (chat) a KV cache TTL of 5-15 minutes is good. For authorization flows that reuse short prefixes, a TTL of 30-60 minutes might be okay. We also support prefix-aware caching where affinity pins particular user or session prefixes to a specific prewarmed host. That reduces the effective cold-start rate but requires consistent hashing work.

[06:20] Renee Cho: what's the effect of batching while maintaining p95 constraints? our support chat can batch a bit but authorizations can't wait.
[06:25] Diego Rivera: we use continuous batching with latency SLO caps per route. For priority routes we set max batch delay to something like 6-10ms or even 0ms for strict latency, and smaller max batch sizes. For best-effort we allow larger delays (up to 50ms) and larger batch sizes. The runtime dynamically trades off batch size vs throughput; we surface recommended profile per route based on your traffic distribution.

[07:10] Samir Patel: what about queueing models — do you support size-limited queues vs time-limited?
[07:15] Olivia Park: yes both. We typically recommend hybrid: limit queue depth to bound memory and tail latency, and also enforce per-request max wait time (deadline) to allow application-level fallbacks. We also add per-priority queue admission controls and a global backpressure multiplier when overall GC or GPU throtting is detected.

[09:00] Aisha Khan: i want to understand the economics: how many reserved GPUs do we need for a 2x day-end spike if we have 5k req/min baseline?
[09:10] Diego Rivera: we'll need to run a burst simulation. Rough rule: estimate sustained tokens/sec for baseline and spike, map to tokens/sec per-GPU given model (we'll ask which model/quantization), and then size for desired headroom. Another pattern: keep reserved capacity for baseline + 20-30% headroom, and rely on ephemeral burst for the remainder if acceptable. For tighter SLOs, reserve more. We'll run the sim with your token-level histogram.

[10:30] Tom Alvarez: what about VPC/on-prem constraints — can bursting to ephemeral instances cross into public cloud? it's a compliance no-no.
[10:35] Olivia Park: for compliance we can keep burst within your VPC or your on-prem datacenter by shipping Redwood Private nodes into your environment. That requires network peering and our private control plane. For true air-gapped, we can deliver an on-prem appliance. The important piece is the ability to spin ephemeral containers on your infrastructure under your IAM/KMS control.

[12:05] Renee Cho: quantization — you've mentioned model variants. how do you manage multi-variant routing? If we route to a quantized model under load how do we manage quality regressions?
[12:12] Diego Rivera: two levers. One is deterministic routing: route to quantized variant only after a threshold (e.g., token latency budget breached AND only for lower-priority routes). Two is canary and QA: Redwood Optimize can run sample set evals in real-time and assess quality drift. We recommend you provide critical prompt set for authorizations. For support chat, 8-bit quantization often has negligible quality impact; for authorization decisions we recommend evaluating mixed-precision (8-bit weights + 16-bit critical layers) or low-rank quantization with retraining if needed.

[14:20] Aisha Khan: what's the fastest safe switching path? we need fallback to a smaller quantized model without manual redeploys.
[14:25] Diego Rivera: we support runtime-compatible variants: same model architecture exported in different quantization profiles. The router can fall back to a quantized variant that is guaranteed to accept the same API signatures; the runtime handles kernel selection. The complexity is ensuring you have prewarmed a quantized variant; fallback to a cold quantized model still costs you a cold-start. So part of policy is to keep a tiny prewarmed footprint of each variant.

[16:00] Maya Chen: on observability, what traces and metrics do you need from HeliosPay to make good prewarm sizing suggestions?
[16:05] Diego Rivera: token-level latency histograms by route, concurrency per-user and per-route, sequence length distribution, and p95/p99 by hour-of-day. Also peak arrival rates over 1/5/15 minute windows, and failure/retry behavior. With those we can compute expected queue depths for a given pool size via M/M/c or G/G/c approximations and then calibrate with Redwood's simulator for fractional batching and KV cache warmup effects.

[18:40] Samir Patel: do you have a sample queueing model we can look at or a spreadsheet?
[18:45] Diego Rivera: yes we'll send a model. It uses an M/G/c baseline with adjustments for batching (effective service time reduces with batch) and a separate function that models cold-start penalty as a function of cold fraction and warmup rate. We'll include parameters you can tweak.

[20:10] Tom Alvarez: regarding KV cache eviction — how do you measure cache hit rate and expose it to us?
[20:15] Olivia Park: runtime emits per-host cache hit/miss rates, per-prefix counts, and estimated memory used. We also emit per-request whether it was a cache hit and the number of KV lookups. We can expose streaming metrics to your observability stack (Prometheus/Datadog) and also show a dashboard in Redwood Console for TTL tuning.

[22:30] Renee Cho: i'm worried about tokenization differences between our preprocessing and Redwood's runtime — could that affect prefix cache effectiveness?
[22:35] Diego Rivera: yes it can. We recommend aligning tokenization offline; Redwood supports multiple tokenizers but the cache is tokenizer-specific. If you use subtle differences, identical semantic prefixes may not hit cache. We'll validate tokenization on a small sample and surface mismatches.

[24:50] Aisha Khan: about prewarming: is synthetic warmup via replay safe from a data governance POV? we can't replay PII.
[24:55] Olivia Park: good point. You can generate synthetic prefix traffic that approximates distribution without PII, or replay only hashed/contextless prefixes. Another option is to use zero-prefix warmup which warms kernels and weights without seeding KV with real user data — it's less cache-effective but safer. We can run both in tandem.

[27:00] Maya Chen: let's talk about a concrete POC shape. Diego?
[27:05] Diego Rivera: propose a 2-week POC: 1) Redwood runs burst sim on your traffic profile and produces a recommended pool sizing and prewarm TTLs; 2) Set up a reserved GPU pool sized for baseline authorizations with small prewarmed footprint for quantized variant; 3) Run controlled spike tests (k8s load generator in your VPC) to validate p95/p99; 4) Collect metrics and tune batch/delay settings. We'll provide a runbook and dashboard.

[30:30] Samir Patel: how intrusive is the reserved pool setup into our network? what firewall rules?
[30:35] Olivia Park: we need outbound HTTPS to Redwood control plane for telemetry and the private agents need internal connectivity to the GPUs. For VPC mode we can use VPC peering or a private link. We'll provide exact IP ranges and the agent container image SHA. No internet-facing ingress required for on-prem.

[33:00] Renee Cho: any known gotchas with mixed quantization and prefix affinity?
[33:05] Diego Rivera: affinity can complicate standardized routing. If you pin prefixes to prewarmed hosts, and then route some traffic to quantized variants elsewhere, you may lose the affinity benefits. For that reason we recommend keeping a small prewarmed footprint of the quantized variant so fallback is fast. Also watch out for warmed kernel mismatch on different GPU types; we recommend homogenous GPU families per pool when predictable latency matters.

[36:10] Aisha Khan: what about autoscaling cooldowns? we tuned some long delays that caused thrashing historically.
[36:15] Diego Rivera: Redwood autoscaling supports hysteresis and predictive scalers. We prefer a two-tier policy: reactive scale-up fast (short cooldown, aggressive) but scale-down slow (longer cooldown) and a predictive scaler that uses hourly patterns to pre-stage capacity ahead of expected peaks. That reduces cold-starts.

[38:05] Tom Alvarez: how do we test tail p99 without inducing cost-prohibitive hours?
[38:10] Diego Rivera: we run targeted tail tests: drive a short-duration heavy spike that simulates worst-case concurrency and measure p99. Also synthetic trace replay with sequence lengths sampled from your histogram lets us estimate tail without running large scale long tests.

[40:30] Samir Patel: what telemetry thresholds would trigger a policy change or fallback to quantized variant?
[40:35] Olivia Park: a common pattern: if p95 > SLO or token compute utilization > 85% for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows, route new best-effort traffic to quantized variants and notify. For priority traffic we prefer to triage: either route to a smaller model variant with verified accuracy or open a short headroom window if tokens/sec drops.

[43:00] Renee Cho: a smaller note - GC pauses on some older CUDA drivers caused jitter for another vendor. Any driver compatibility notes for reserved on-prem GPUs?
[43:05] Diego Rivera: ensure modern NVIDIA drivers and CUDA compatible with our runtime. We provide validated driver/OS stacks. For older drivers you might see sporadic pauses. We'll include a compatibility matrix in the docs we share.

[45:20] Maya Chen: wrapping up - recap of agreed items?
[45:25] Aisha Khan: agreed to POC scope and data upload for burst sim.
[45:30] Samir Patel: will upload token-level histograms and traffic traces to the shared S3.
[45:33] Diego Rivera: we'll run the simulation and share a sizing spreadsheet, plus recommended prewarm TTLs and batch profiles. We'll also provide a set of YAMLs for reserved pool agent deploy.

[46:10] Tom Alvarez: one last question - does Redwood expose the per-request kv-cache hit flag so we can tie regressions to cache misses?
[46:15] Olivia Park: yes, per-request metadata includes cache_hit: true/false and number_of_kv_lookups. We'll stream that.

[48:00] Aisha Khan: thanks everyone. Next steps/timeframe?
[48:05] Maya Chen: we'll target the deliverables in the next 5 business days for the simulation and schedule POC kickoff week of 2026-04-27.

[48:30] Renee Cho: sounds good, thanks.
[48:35] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the S3 link and the runbook.

[48:40] [meeting ends]
